newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy hopes to make it third time lucky on reform.
newsitem.headline: Italy hopes to make it third time lucky on reform.

text.p: A government plan to start reforming Italy's outdated constitution moved into the home straight on Wednesday after the opposition centre-right coalition mended internal splits and promised its backing.
The Senate (upper house) began its second reading of a bill to set up a bi-cameral commission to propose changes to the 1948 document and was due to vote on Thursday morning.
"The prospects for the bi-cameral commission are good," Post and Communications Minister Antonio Maccanico told reporters.
The centre-left government, which says it has a historical duty to reform Italy, hopes to make it third time lucky.
Two previous bi-cameral committees have failed and big corruption scandals in the early 1990s, which swept away the old governing class, also failed to usher in a new era of change.

Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi summoned his partners in the centre-right Freedom Alliance on Tuesday to hammer out a unified stance after far-right leader Gianfranco Fini threatened to scupper the bi-cameral commission's chances of being born.

Berlusconi, who has negotiated closely with Massimo D'Alema, the head of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left and the main architecht of the plan, managed to wring a compromise out of Fini and all sides emerged smiling and promising support.
That should now ensure that the bill is carried by a comfortable two-thirds majority, the threshold needed to pass directly into law without having to be put to a referendum.

The Senate vote will be followed by a vote in the lower Chamber of Deputies on Tuesday or Wednesday, now apparently just a formality. The 70-member body should be up and running in early February and will have until June 30 to draft its changes.
"Now the ball's in D'Alema's court," said Gustavo Selva, a senior member of Fini's National Alliance party. D'Alema is widely tipped as a front runner to chair the commission.
Both the government and opposition agree that big modifications are needed to the form and powers of government, the size of the parliament and the country's regional structure.

Berlusconi apparently won a key concession from Fini at their meeting on Tuesday to back his demand for the prime minister to be elected directly. Fini had previously favoured a semi-presidential, French style system.

However, the centre-left Popular Party which sponsored Prime Minister Romano Prodi wants a system under which the prime minister would not be elected directly but a likely prime ministerial candidate would be "indicated" to the electorate.

Under the current republican constitution that structured the state after the abolition of the monarchy and was intended to bolster democracy in the wake of Fascism, only the president can appoint the prime minister and dissolve parliament.

Both left and right agree that the 630-member Chamber is too big and the 325-member Senate, whose functions duplicate those of the lower house, should be remodelled as a smaller Chamber of Regions to strengthen Italy's federal make-up.
De-centralisation is another urgent task, given added impetus last year by separatist leader Umberto Bossi's proclamation of a self-styled "Republic of the North".
Changes to Italy's convoluted electoral system -- currently a mix of first-past-the-post and proportional representation -- could also be enshrined in the new constitution.
The committtee will report back to parliament with its proposals, which will put to a referendum before becoming law.
